characterList.description: A dark gray, rocky exoplanet with a rough and fragmented surface.
characterList.name: Kepler 70c

characterList.description: A smaller, similarly dark gray exoplanet, also with a rocky surface.
characterList.name: Kepler 70b

content_metadata.description: Video Analysis of Kepler 70c: A Zombie Planet

qAndA.answer: The surface is composed of highly compressed, molten metals, giving it a dark, shiny, and brittle appearance.
qAndA.question: What is unique about the surface of Kepler 70c?

qAndA.answer: The "rivers" are formed by the accumulation of debris that continuously fall and cluster together due to the planet's gravity.
qAndA.question: What is responsible for the "rivers" of asteroids seen on Kepler 70c?

qAndA.answer: The gravitational tides produce violent rock storms that send debris flying into space. This debris gets trapped within the orbital paths of the two planets, forming a giant ring around the star.
qAndA.question: What happens when Kepler 70b passes close to Kepler 70c?

qAndA.answer: They are referred to as "zombie planets" because they survived the destruction of their gaseous outer layers when their host star expanded into a red giant. Only their dense metal cores remain, continuing to orbit the star like remnants of their former selves.
qAndA.question: Why are Kepler 70c and Kepler 70b called "zombie planets"?

qAndA.answer: The video evokes a sense of awe, wonder, and curiosity. It presents a captivating look at a bizarre and unfamiliar world that challenges our perception of planets and highlights the unpredictable nature of the cosmos. The visuals and narration work together to create a sense of discovery and invite viewers to contemplate the vastness and strangeness of the universe.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: What you are now seeing is the exoplanet Kepler-70C.
It was formerly called K-O-I-55C.
Kepler-70C and its brother planet Kepler-70B are two silent survivors and evidence of the
brutality of the cosmos.
Somewhere around 18 million years ago, these two planets were probably a pair of gas giants
orbiting Kepler-70, which was their host star.
When the star passed through its red giant state, it engulfed the two planets and consumed
them in the process, leaving only their high-density metal cores orbiting the system, like two
zombies.
Kepler-70C registers high temperatures, but as it is tidally locked, we can explore the
dark side of a planet.
Nevertheless, the bizarre landscape has a strange beauty.
All of the surface is composed of highly compressed melted metals, giving it the appearance of a
shiny, brittle dark skin.
Due to the violent process it suffered, the planet is full of scars and millions and millions
of pieces continually float around like an angry swarm.
The gravity makes the floating rocks swirl and cluster in capricious ways.
Now we find a canyon, and we surf a river of asteroids.
Now we see valleys, terraces, hills and mountains.
Now, we find clouds made of rocks and dust covering an ocean of metallic dunes.
And sometimes we can see Kepler-70B passing through the dark sky, as the two planets
pass each other.
At its closest point, there are only 240,000 kilometers apart.
When this happens, the gravity tides produce violent rock storms that send debris to the
space that becomes trapped inside the two planets orbit, drawing a giant ring around the
star.

youtube_description:
Artistic depiction of Kepler 70c (KOI55c)  in the Kepler 70 system, along with Kepler 70b. Somewhere around 18 million years ago, these two planets were probably a pair of gas giants orbiting Kepler 70 which was their host star.  When the star passed through its red giant state, it engulfed the two planets and consumed them in the process leaving only their high density metal cores orbiting the system like two zombies.
The project is all modeled with Houdini 16, except some parts with Cinema 4D. Everything is set and rendered  in Clarisse iFX. 

DISCLAIMER: The art material contained in this channel is pure speculation. It is NOT true. It is based and INSPIRED on data obtained from different scientific information available to the general public. In other words -or reading between lines if you want- The art displayed here is not meant to be scientifically accurate or educational per se, although I try to not make it just entertaining or beautiful but also educational. I hope that this does not sound paradoxical.
